idiom_name: trait CustomerDao with a JDBC implementation returning Option/case classes
implementation_notes: Scala's trait gives the DAO the same shape as the Java original and JDBC is reached through Java interop, so the classic form is a trait plus an implementation class holding a DataSource and mapping ResultSet rows into case classes, which are returned as Option/List so no cursor escapes. What replaces hand-written plumbing is the collections library: rows are sequenced into immutable values inside the DAO. Keep this blocking form for thread-based services or when plain JDBC should stay visible; the tagless-final variant below is the usual choice in a functional Scala stack.
pitfalls: Blocking JDBC inside a Future or an effect without a dedicated blocking pool starves the compute pool; either mark the call site or use the tagless-final variant with its own execution context.
ResultSet is mutable and connection-bound: rows must be sequenced into case classes inside the same connection scope, otherwise the values are lost when the connection returns to the pool.
Scala's Java collections interop hides nulls from Java APIs: wrap Option around nullable driver reads (rs.getString) instead of trusting them.

variants.name: Tagless-final DAO described in ConnectionIO with doobie
variants.idiom_name: sql"...".query[Customer].option composed in ConnectionIO, run by transact(xa)
variants.implementation_notes: doobie is a pure functional JDBC layer for Scala and Cats, not an ORM: statements are values of type ConnectionIO that are composed purely and executed only by transact(xa) on a Transactor, so the DAO becomes a set of descriptions (or a trait parameterised over F[_]) whose effects are declared rather than performed. Choose it when the application already runs Cats Effect or another Typelevel stack and connection management should be declarative; keep the plain JDBC trait when no effect system is present, because ConnectionIO without the surrounding runtime is just indirection.
pitfalls: ConnectionIO must be executed with transact on a Transactor: a DAO method that transacts internally cannot compose with the caller's transaction.
Transactors and connection pools are cats-effect Resources; blocking with unsafeRunSync inside the DAO (or leaking the Resource) breaks cancellation and pool reuse.
